ai.literal: Not despising the power of those who can accomplish deeds, among all the protections of those who protect themselves, is the foremost.
ai.translation: Not disregarding the power of those who can accomplish great deeds is the foremost of all safeguards for those who wish to protect themselves.
ai.modern: காரியங்களைச் சாதிக்க வல்லவர்களின் ஆற்றலை இகழாமல் இருப்பது, தம்மைக் காக்க நினைப்பவர்கள் செய்யும் பாதுகாப்புகள் எல்லாவற்றிலும் முதன்மையானது ஆகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the supreme importance of self-preservation through respect. The word 'ஆற்றுவார்' refers to capable people who have the power to execute great tasks, and 'ஆற்றல்' is their inherent strength. The poet explains that for those who wish to guard themselves ('போற்றுவார்') from ruin, avoiding the disrespect or slighting ('இகழாமை') of such powerful individuals is the most vital ('தலை') of all protective measures ('போற்றலுள் எல்லாம்'). True safety begins not with physical fortresses, but with the wisdom of not provoking those who possess the power to act.

ai.literal: If one behaves without honoring the great ones, it will bring undeparting suffering by those great ones.
ai.translation: If one conducts oneself without respecting great people, it will bring endless, unremovable distress through those very great ones.
ai.modern: பெரியவர்களை மதிக்காமல் நடந்துகொண்டால், அந்தப் பெரியவர்களாலேயே நீங்காத துன்பம் உண்டாகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet warns of the severe consequences of disrespecting or neglecting wise and powerful elders. If a person behaves without due regard or reverence for them, it triggers ruinous distress. This suffering is described as 'pērā', meaning it is permanent and cannot be easily removed or escaped. Crucially, this inescapable ruin is brought about by the power and influence of the very great ones who were offended.

ai.literal: If ruin is desired, act without listening; if destruction is desired, commit offense towards those who are capable of action.
ai.translation: If one desires ruin, let them act without listening to advice; if they desire swift destruction, let them commit an offense against those who have the power to act.
ai.modern: ஒருவர் தன் அழிவை விரும்பினால், நல்லோர் அறிவுரையைக் கேட்காமல் செயல்படட்டும்; தன் முடிவை விரும்பினால், ஆற்றல் மிக்கவர்களிடம் தவறு செய்யட்டும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet uses powerful irony to warn against self-destructive behavior. The poet suggests that if a person is determined to ruin themselves, they can simply act blindly without listening to any wise counsel. However, if they want to guarantee their immediate and complete destruction, they should go a step further and offend those who possess great power and capability. The word 'āṟṟupavar' highlights individuals who have the strength and means to execute actions, while 'iḻukku' refers to the fatal mistake of transgressing against them.

ai.literal: Doing harm to those who are powerful by those who are powerless is like beckoning the God of Death with one's own hand.
ai.translation: For the weak to do harm to the powerful is like beckoning the God of Death with one's own hand.
ai.modern: வலிமை உடையவர்களுக்கு வலிமையற்றவர்கள் தீங்கு செய்வது, எமனைத் தன் கையால் கூவி அழைப்பதற்கு ஒப்பானதாகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet warns against the extreme danger of provoking or offending those who possess great power. The poet compares a weak person ('āṟṟādār') trying to harm a powerful person ('āṟṟuvār') to someone beckoning the God of Death ('kūṟṟam') with their own hand ('kaiyāl viḷittatṟāl'). Such an act is not just a mistake, but an active invitation to one's own swift and certain destruction.

ai.literal: Where having gone, anywhere they exist will not become, fierce of strength king by whom angered against.
ai.translation: Those who have incurred the wrath of a king of fierce power will not survive, wherever they go, even if they flee to any place.
ai.modern: கடும் வலிமை கொண்ட அரசனால் வெறுக்கப்பட்டு அழிக்கப்பட்டவர்கள், எங்குச் சென்றாலும் எங்கும் உயிர் பிழைத்து வாழ முடியாது.
ai.explanation: This couplet warns of the inescapable consequences of provoking those in supreme power. The phrase 'வெந்துப்பின் வேந்து' describes a ruler of fierce, burning might. Those who become the target of such a ruler's wrath ('செறப்பட்டவர்') cannot find safety anywhere. No matter where they flee ('யாண்டுச் சென்று'), they will not survive ('யாண்டும் உளராகார்') because the reach of a mighty sovereign is absolute.

ai.literal: By fire even if burnt, escape there may be; they will not escape, great ones having offended who behave.
ai.translation: Even if one is burnt by fire, there may be a way to survive; but those who behave offensively towards great people will never escape destruction.
ai.modern: நெருப்பினால் சுடப்பட்டாலும் தப்பிப் பிழைக்க வழி உண்டு; ஆனால், பெரியவர்களுக்குத் தீங்கு செய்து வாழ்பவர்கள் தப்பிப் பிழைக்க மாட்டார்கள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet warns of the absolute ruin that comes from offending great people. The poet uses a powerful contrast with fire: even if a person is physically caught in a fire, there is still a rare chance of survival. However, for those who behave disrespectfully or act against great minds, there is absolutely no escape from ruin. The word 'உய்வு' refers to survival or escape, while 'பிழைத்து' here carries the meaning of committing a wrong or offense. The verse emphasizes that moral and social transgressions against the wise are far more destructive than physical elements.

ai.literal: Of what use will a life excellent in its ways and great wealth become, if worthy ones of excellent virtue become angry?
ai.translation: Of what avail are a life of excellent means and vast wealth, if worthy people of great virtue are provoked to anger?
ai.modern: தகைமை சிறந்த தகுதியுடைய பெரியோர்கள் கோபித்துக் கொண்டால், எல்லா வழிகளிலும் சிறப்புற்ற வாழ்க்கையும், மிகப்பெரிய செல்வமும் இருந்தும் என்ன பயன் தரும்?
ai.explanation: This couplet warns against incurring the wrath of great and worthy people. The word 'takkār' refers to those who are worthy and fit, possessing great virtue ('takai māṇṭa'). If such noble persons are provoked to anger ('ceṟiṉ'), then all the excellent ways of one's life ('vakaimāṇṭa vāḻkkai') and all one's vast wealth ('vāṉporuḷ') will become completely useless ('eṉṉām'). The repetition of 'māṇṭa' (excellent) emphasizes that even the most excellent worldly achievements and possessions cannot save a person from the ruin caused by offending the truly great.

ai.literal: If [one] estimates those who are like a hill so as to diminish [them], those who are like having stood [firmly] will perish on the earth along with [their] family.
ai.translation: If one underestimates and disrespects those who are as great as a mountain, even those who seemed firmly established on this earth will perish along with their entire lineage.
ai.modern: மலை போன்ற பெருமை உடையவர்களைக் குறைவாக மதித்து நடத்தினால், இவ்வுலகில் நிலைபெற்று வாழ்வது போல் தோன்றியவர்களும் தங்கள் குடும்பத்தோடு அழிந்து போவார்கள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet warns against offending or disrespecting great people. The poet compares great people to a mountain (குன்று) in their stability, virtue, and stature. If anyone underestimates (குன்ற மதிப்பின்) or treats these mountain-like individuals with disrespect, the consequences are catastrophic. Even those who seemed firmly established and secure on this earth (நின்றன்னார்) will completely perish, not just individually, but along with their entire family or lineage (குடியொடு).

ai.literal: If those of lofty principles rage, even the king, breaking in the middle, his kingship will perish.
ai.translation: If men of lofty principles flare up in anger, even a mighty king will be broken midway and lose his kingdom.
ai.modern: உயர்ந்த கொள்கைகளை உடைய பெரியோர்கள் கோபமடைந்தால், பெரும் அரசனும்கூட நடுவிலேயே முறிந்து தன் அரசாட்சியை இழந்து அழிவான்.
ai.explanation: This couplet warns of the catastrophic consequences of provoking highly principled and self-controlled people. 'ஏந்திய கொள்கையார்' refers to those who steadfastly uphold noble vows and high moral principles. If such great people are driven to righteous anger ('சீறின்'), even a supreme ruler ('வேந்தனும்') will see his power snap in the middle ('இடைமுரிந்து') like a tree in a storm. Ultimately, both the king and his entire kingdom ('வேந்து') will be completely ruined.

ai.literal: Even if they possess boundlessly established support, they will not escape, if those of excellently established greatness become angry.
ai.translation: Even if they possess boundless and powerful support, they will not escape ruin if those of eminent and established greatness become angry.
ai.modern: மிகவும் சிறந்த பாதுகாப்பைப் பெற்றிருந்தாலும், சிறந்த பெருமைகளை உடைய பெரியவர்கள் கோபமடைந்தால், அவர்களிடமிருந்து தப்பிப் பிழைக்க முடியாது.
ai.explanation: This couplet warns against provoking the wrath of highly realized, great individuals. Even if a person has immense, seemingly invincible worldly support (சார்பு) from kings, armies, or wealth, it will not save them from ruin. If those who possess eminent and established greatness (சீரார்) are provoked to anger (செறின்), the offender cannot escape (உய்யார்) destruction. The contrast between worldly protection and the spiritual power of the great shows that moral and spiritual force always triumphs over material strength.
